technical.prompt: What is a market-cap-weighted index?

choices.answer: An index weighting companies by their market value
distractors: An index giving each company equal weight
An index weighted by share price
An index weighted by employee count

technical.prompt: What is an equal-weighted index?

choices.answer: An index giving every constituent the same weight
distractors: An index weighted by market value
An index weighted by share price

technical.prompt: In a price-weighted average, which stocks have the most influence, and why is that a weakness?

choices.answer: High-priced stocks, regardless of company size
distractors: The largest companies by market value
Every stock equally, whatever its price
The stocks with the most employees

technical.prompt: What is free-float adjustment?
expectedPoints: Counts only shares available to trade

choices.answer: Counting only shares that are freely available to trade

technical.prompt: What is an index divisor?
expectedPoints: Number used to compute index level

choices.answer: A number adjusted so corporate actions don't jump the index
distractors: The number of stocks in an index
The dividend paid by the index

technical.prompt: What is the difference between price return and total return indices?

choices.answer: Total return adds reinvested dividends

technical.prompt: What is index reconstitution?

choices.answer: A scheduled review of which stocks are included

technical.prompt: What are capping rules in an index?

choices.answer: Limits on how much weight any one constituent can have
distractors: Limits on the number of indices

technical.prompt: What is a factor or smart beta index?
expectedPoints: Weights by factors like value or momentum

choices.answer: A rules-based index tilted to factors like value
distractors: An index built entirely by AI
An index of technology companies only
An index that follows no rules

technical.prompt: What is a custom index?

choices.answer: An index built to one client's specification
distractors: An index that anyone can change

technical.prompt: What is asset-based index licensing?
expectedPoints: Fee as share of product assets

choices.answer: A licence fee charged as a share of a product's assets
distractors: A fee charged per page of data
A flat annual fee per user
A fee charged on each trade only

technical.prompt: What is the difference between display and non-display data use?
expectedPoints: Display: shown on screens to people

choices.answer: Display is shown to people; non-display feeds machines

technical.prompt: What is a redistribution licence?
expectedPoints: Right to pass data to others

choices.answer: A licence to pass data on to clients
distractors: A licence to move to new offices
A licence to split an index in two
A licence to trade index futures

technical.prompt: What is reference data?

choices.answer: Descriptive details like terms and identifiers

technical.prompt: What is the difference between real-time and delayed data?

choices.answer: Real-time is instant; delayed is later and cheaper
distractors: Both arrive at exactly the same time

technical.prompt: What is survivorship bias in financial data?

choices.answer: Leaving out failed firms, which flatters returns
distractors: A bias found only in insurance data

technical.prompt: Why do benchmark administrators need oversight committees?

choices.answer: To review methodology independently and manage conflicts
distractors: To set the index's price each day
To pick stocks for fund managers

technical.prompt: What is an ESG index?
expectedPoints: Selects or weights by ESG criteria

choices.answer: An index screening or weighting on ESG
distractors: An index of energy stocks only
An index of emerging markets only
An index that follows no rules

technical.prompt: Why does data quality matter so much to a data provider?
expectedPoints: Clients rely on it for decisions

choices.answer: Clients trade and value assets on it

technical.prompt: An index holds three companies with market caps of $300 billion, $100 billion and $100 billion. What are their weights?
expectedPoints: Weights show each company's influence on returns

technical.prompt: A company has 1 billion shares at $50, and 40% are held by its founder. What is its float-adjusted market cap?

choices.answer: $30 billion

technical.prompt: A price-weighted index holds stocks at $100, $50 and $30, with a divisor of 3. What is the index level?
Three stocks return 10%, 0% and -4%. With 60/20/20 cap weights, what are the equal-weighted and cap-weighted returns?

choices.answer: 2% equal-weighted; 5.2% cap-weighted

technical.prompt: Funds tracking an index hold $1 trillion. A stock added at 0.5% weight trades $1 billion a day. How much must funds buy, and how many days' volume is that?

choices.answer: About $5 billion, or five days of volume

technical.prompt: An index's constituents total $1,000 billion with a divisor of 10. A $50 billion company is replaced by a $70 billion one. What new divisor keeps the level unchanged?
A rebalance moves 5% of an index's weight out of some stocks and into others. Funds tracking it hold $200 billion. How much do they trade in total, counting both buys and sells?

choices.answer: About $20 billion

technical.prompt: 200 firms each pay $100,000 a year for non-display data use. What is the revenue?
expectedPoints: Revenue scales with the number of licensed firms

choices.answer: About $20 million

technical.prompt: A data business has 5% annual churn and raises prices 4%. Ignoring new customers, how does revenue change?

choices.answer: It falls about 1.2%

technical.prompt: A stock would be 40% of a sector index with a 25% cap. What happens?

choices.answer: It's cut to 25%, with the excess spread to others
distractors: It is removed from the index

technical.prompt: Why do equal-weighted indices have higher turnover than cap-weighted ones?

choices.answer: They must trim winners and top up losers

technical.prompt: How does a stock split affect a price-weighted index?

choices.answer: Its weight falls and the divisor is cut
distractors: Its weight in the index doubles

technical.prompt: Why is asset-based licensing attractive to index providers?

choices.answer: Revenue grows with fund assets at low cost
distractors: It stays fixed regardless of assets
It falls as fund assets grow
It needs a large sales team

technical.prompt: Why do index providers consult the market before methodology changes?

choices.answer: Changes move huge sums, so users get a say
distractors: Changes have no effect on funds

technical.prompt: Why do back-tests need point-in-time data?

choices.answer: To use only information that was available at the time

technical.prompt: Why have factor indices grown in popularity?

choices.answer: They offer cheap, rules-based factor exposure
distractors: They follow no rules at all
They cost more than active funds

technical.prompt: What is derived data, and why do providers charge for it?

choices.answer: New figures built from licensed data
distractors: Data that's entirely free to use

technical.prompt: What conflicts of interest can an index provider face?
expectedPoints: Owned by an exchange or asset manager
